steps.text: Black's pawn has just jumped past yours, off the square you attack. Can you still take it? Sometimes yes, but only right now. This lesson shows when, why the rule exists, and when it does not apply. [R] The rule is in the FIDE Laws of Chess, recalled and not re-read here. No coach's view is used in this lesson.

Black's pawn has not moved yet, so it may jump two squares to d5. Look at what stands beside d5: White's pawn on e5. That pawn attacks d6, but it does not attack d5, so the jump slips past it. Chess has a special rule for this moment. Watch it happen on the board first, then we will name it.

steps.caption: Black jumps past White's pawn. White gets one chance to answer.

line.say: Black's pawn jumps two squares and lands beside White's pawn, past the square White attacks.
White captures as if the pawn had stepped one square: it lands on d6 and the pawn on d5 is removed.

claims.statement: The jump to d5 is legal.

steps.caption: Compare: what if Black had stepped only one square?

line.say: Stepping one square lands on d6, which White's pawn attacks.
White simply captures it. The special rule gives White this same capture after the jump.

claims.statement: The one-step move is legal.

steps.text: That is **en passant**, French for 'in passing'. When a pawn jumps two squares and lands right beside an enemy pawn, that pawn may capture it as if it had stepped only one square. [I] Our reading of why the rule exists: it stops the two-square jump from being a way to dodge a capture.

Three small facts. The capture is optional: you may take it or play something else. The capturing pawn always stands on its own fifth rank, counting from your side: rank 5 for White, rank 4 for Black. And 'beside' means the same rank, one file over, on either side.

steps.caption: Both are legal. You may capture on d6 or simply step ahead; the choice is yours.

claims.statement: Capturing en passant is legal.
Stepping ahead is legal too, so the capture is optional.

steps.caption: The same idea for Black: White jumps, Black answers.

line.say: White's pawn jumps two squares and lands beside Black's pawn.
Black captures en passant: the pawn lands on e3 and the white pawn on e4 is removed.

claims.statement: The jump to e4 is legal.

steps.caption: Black has just jumped to d5. The empty square it passed over is d6: that is where your capturing pawn lands.

claims.statement: The pawn on e5 can step to e6 or capture en passant on d6.

steps.caption: Pawns on the edge of the board jump too. Only one neighbour can reply.

line.say: The rook-file pawn jumps and lands beside White's pawn on b5.
White captures en passant on a6, the square the jumper passed over.

claims.statement: The jump to a5 is legal.

steps.caption: Black has just jumped to c5, between two white pawns. Either may capture; you choose one.

line.say: The pawn from b5 captures. The pawn on d5 could have done it instead, but only one capture is made.

claims.statement: The pawn on b5 can capture en passant.
The pawn on d5 can capture en passant too.

steps.text: Before you decide, ask three questions about your opponent's **last** move. Was it a pawn? Did it move two squares? Did it land right beside one of my pawns? Three yes answers mean the capture is available this turn, as long as it does not leave your own king in check. You do not have to take it. [H] Asking the questions after every pawn jump may build the habit faster than remembering the rule. We have no data on that yet.

steps.caption: White ignores the chance and moves the king. A move later the chance is gone.

line.say: White plays a different move and does not capture.
Black replies. The pawn on d5 now stands beside White's pawn in an ordinary way: the chance has passed.

claims.statement: Capturing en passant is legal in this position, right now.

steps.caption: Two moves later. Nothing is wrong with the pawns, but the chance is gone.

claims.statement: Capturing en passant is no longer legal.

steps.title: Same pawns, one change
steps.prompt: Black has just jumped a pawn to d5, or it was standing there already. Predict first: can White capture en passant?

steps.text: The right exists only straight after the jump, and only for a pawn beside the jumper. It fails in three ways: your pawn is not beside it (including a jumper that lands diagonally ahead of your pawn, which you take with an ordinary capture), the enemy pawn stepped only once, or you waited a move. In each case you have only your ordinary moves.

steps.caption: Black jumps, but White's pawn is two files away, so it is not beside the jumper.

line.say: Black jumps to d5. White's pawn on f5 is not beside it.
White's pawn can only step ahead. There is nothing to capture.

claims.statement: The jump to d5 is legal.

steps.caption: Black jumps onto a square White's pawn already attacks.

line.say: Black's pawn lands diagonally ahead of White's pawn, not beside it.
White takes it in the ordinary way. No special rule is needed.

claims.statement: The jump to d5 is legal.

steps.caption: Black steps one square and lands beside White's pawn. A step is not a jump.

line.say: Black's pawn takes one step and lands beside White's pawn.
White's pawn can only walk ahead. There is no capture, because Black did not jump.

claims.statement: The one-step move is legal.

steps.caption: Black has just jumped to c5. All the usual conditions are met, but the capture is not allowed.

line.say: White walks the pawn ahead instead, since capturing would expose the king.

claims.statement: The en passant capture is not legal here.
The pawn can still step ahead.

steps.text: Why does the rule exist? [I] Our reading: without it, a pawn on its start square could jump past an enemy pawn that would have captured a one-step move. The jump would be a free way to dodge the capture. The rule gives back the capture the step would have allowed. Compare the two boards.

steps.caption: Without the rule [I]: the jump slips past, and White's pawn can only walk on.

line.say: Black jumps beside White's pawn.
White can only step ahead. The jumper escaped a capture that a one-step move would have met.

claims.statement: The jump is legal.

steps.caption: A careless jump walks into the rule.

line.say: Black jumps without asking what the jump allows.
White captures en passant. The pawn on d6 gives check and also attacks the rook on c7.
The king must leave the check. It cannot take the pawn on d6, because the rook on d1 guards it.
The pawn takes the rook.
The king takes the pawn, but White has won a rook and a pawn for one pawn.

claims.statement: The jump is legal.
The jump is a mistake: it is worse than the best move by at least three pawns' worth.

steps.text: Look for the fork. The pawn that captures en passant lands on a new square and can attack two things at once, often the king and a rook. Next, find the capture.

steps.caption: The jump itself gives check. En passant is a legal answer that removes the checker.

line.say: The jump lands beside Black's pawn and attacks the king.
Black captures en passant and the checking pawn is removed.

claims.statement: The jump is legal.

steps.text: In a game score the capture is written like an ordinary capture with a tag, for example dxc6 e.p. The tag tells you the captured pawn was not on the landing square. Now watch it on a board.

steps.caption: The score would read 'dxc6 e.p.' after the jump.

line.say: Black jumps beside White's pawn.
White captures en passant, landing on c6.

claims.statement: The jump is legal.

steps.caption: How the rule can arise from the starting position. We built this legal sequence to show the pattern; it is not a claim about good play.

line.say: White plays e4.
Black plays e6. [I] Our guess at the purpose: to contest the middle with a pawn on d5 next.
White advances again; the pawn now stands where a black d-pawn jump would land beside it.
Black jumps and lands beside White's pawn.
White may capture en passant here.

claims.statement: The first move is legal.

steps.text: **A model explanation to check yours against.** En passant is an optional pawn capture that exists only on the move right after an enemy pawn jumps two squares and lands right beside your pawn. You capture it as if it had stepped one square, landing on the square it passed over. If you wait a move, if it only stepped once, or if it was not beside your pawn, the chance is gone. It is also illegal if it would leave your own king in check.

steps.prompt: Explain en passant to a friend who has never heard of it. Cover the three questions, how long the chance lasts, and one case where the capture is not allowed. Say it aloud or write it, without looking back.
